title: The Fraud Model That Never Flags Fraud
scenario: A bank builds a model to flag fraudulent transactions. Out of 100,000 transactions, only 400 (0.4%) are actually fraudulent. The team's first model reports 99.6% accuracy on the test set, and everyone is thrilled - until someone points out the model predicts 'not fraud' for every single transaction.
question: Which single metric would have caught this problem immediately, before anyone needed to inspect individual predictions?

options.explanation: This is exactly the metric that hid the problem. Because 99.6% of transactions are legitimate, a model that always predicts 'not fraud' still scores 99.6% accuracy - the metric is dominated by the majority class and says nothing about whether any fraud was ever caught.

Precision-Recall AUC focuses specifically on how well the model finds the positive (fraud) class, which is what actually matters here. A model that never predicts fraud would have zero recall and a PR-AUC near the baseline fraud rate, immediately exposing the problem that accuracy hid.

ROC-AUC is a reasonable metric to also track, but with such extreme imbalance it can look deceptively good because the false-positive rate stays low even when recall on the tiny fraud class is poor - the large number of true negatives dominates. PR-AUC is more sensitive to performance specifically on the rare positive class.

MSE is an error metric for continuous/regression predictions. Fraud detection here is a classification problem (fraud vs. not fraud), so MSE is not the natural fit, and it would not have flagged the all-negative model's failure any more clearly than accuracy would.

key_takeaway: For severely imbalanced classification, accuracy is close to meaningless - its value is dominated by the majority class. Metrics that isolate performance on the minority/positive class (PR-AUC, recall, F1 at a chosen threshold) are what actually reveal whether the model is doing its job.
common_misconception: Treating a single 'accuracy' number as sufficient evidence a classifier works, without checking the class distribution first.

experimentation.objective: Simulate a highly imbalanced fraud dataset, score a trivial 'always predict not-fraud' classifier, and compute accuracy vs. PR-AUC/recall side by side to see how differently they score the same (useless) model.
experimentation.data_generation_code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification

X, y = make_classification(
    n_samples=100_000,
    n_features=10,
    weights=[0.996, 0.004],   # ~0.4% fraud, matches the scenario
    flip_y=0.01,
    random_state=42,
)
